articles.title: An information theoretic approach to evaluating social behaviour in mice using automated home-cage monitoring
articles.content: Background: Social behaviour in mice is commonly assessed using standardized assays such as the three-chambered task, which provide controlled measures of sociability but often capture behaviour over short timeframes that may not capture the complex behavioural repertoire exhibited in the home environment. Although automated home-cage monitoring enables continuous, longitudinal assessment of group-housed mice with minimal human interference, methods for quantifying social behaviour in this complex setting remain limited. Information theory offers a framework for measuring statistical dependence between animals but requires one to account for dependence related to the cage environment that arise even in the absence of social interaction. Methods: We developed an information-theoretic approach to quantify social dependence using longitudinal RFID-based positional data from group-housed mice monitored with automated home-cage monitoring system. Mutual information (MI) between cagemates was evaluated against a constrained null model that disrupted within-cage dependence while preserving individual movement patterns. We used two strains with known differences in sociability (C57BL/6J and BTBR) to assess sensitivity to various temporal sampling parameters, test-retest reliability, and correspondence with manually video-scored social behaviours. We further examined variation across genetic backgrounds and investigated relationships between home-cage measures, conventional behavioural assays (three-chamber sociability and open-field behaviour), and brain structure using in vivo MRI. Results: Observed MI was distinguishable from our null distribution, validating its use to quantify statistical dependence beyond that expected from shared cage constraints. MI recapitulated known differences in sociability between C57BL/6J and BTBR mice, showed high test-retest reliability, and correlated with independently video-scored social behaviours. Home-cage social measures also varied across genetic backgrounds and captured strain differences separate from three-chamber sociability. Furthermore, in vivo MRI revealed distinct neuroanatomical patterns for home cage compared to three-chamber sociability measures, including brain regions implicated in social behaviour. Comparisons with open-field measures further indicated that home-cage information-theoretic measures capture behavioural variation not fully represented by conventional measures of locomotion and exploration. Finally, social coordination exhibited distinct temporal dynamics across the circadian cycle. Conclusion: This study establishes and validates an information-theoretic framework for quantifying social dependence from longitudinal home-cage positional data. By accounting for dependence arising from shared environmental constraints and demonstrating reproducibility and correspondence with observed social behaviour, this approach provides a complementary method for characterizing social behaviour in mice. Its application across genetic backgrounds and temporal contexts offers opportunities to investigate behavioural variation beyond the restricted sampling of conventional assays.
articles.author: Chien, T., Fernandes, D. J., Sled, J. G., Lerch, J. P.

articles.title: Correction for age-appropriate relaxation reference values alters estimates of neurometabolite concentration, but not age relationships
articles.content: MRS-measured metabolite concentration estimates in the brain show significant changes over the lifespan. An important step in accurately quantifying metabolite levels using in vivo MRS is correction for T1- and T2- weighting of water and metabolite signals. Despite substantial literature indicating that both T1 and T2 of water and metabolites change across the lifespan, most aging studies use age-invariant reference values in quantification equations. It is important to establish whether observed changes in metabolite levels are driven by relaxation effects or actual concentration changes. In three recent studies, we have characterized changes in water and metabolite relaxation times across the adult lifespan, specifying linear models to predict age-appropriate T1 and T2 values for use in quantification. To establish whether prior metabolite-age correlation findings are driven by age-dependent errors in relaxation corrections, age-appropriate metabolite T1 and T2 values and age- and region-appropriate water T1 and T2 values were applied to re-calculate metabolite levels for a large lifespan cohort. While major metabolite (total N-acetyl aspartate tNAA, total choline tCho, total creatine tCr, myo-inositol mI, glutamate + glutamine Glx) concentration estimates were lower after using an age-appropriate relaxation correction analysis pipeline, the metabolite-age relationships were unchanged. We conclude that well-documented changes in metabolite and water relaxation times across the healthy adult lifespan do not drive findings of metabolite-age correlations.

articles.title: Sex differences in the effects of enhanced adult hippocampal neurogenesis on pattern discrimination and Intellicage spatial learning in Bax-knockout mice
articles.content: Adult hippocampal neurogenesis has been implicated in learning and memory. Although increasing neurogenesis has been associated with improved spatial learning and pattern discrimination, whether these benefits differ between male and female mice remains unclear. The goal of this study was to see if increasing adult hippocampal neurogenesis improves learning in male and female mice, and whether the benefit is the same in both sexes. We used conditional deletion of the pro-apoptotic gene Bax to increase the survival of newborn dentate granule cells. Male and female BAX knockout (KO) and wild-type (WT) mice were tested in Intellicage place learning and reversal learning tasks, and an A/B context discrimination task. BAX KO mice had more tdTomato-positive newborn dentate granule cells than BAX WT mice, with no significant effect of sex. During Intellicage adaptation, there were no differences between genotypes or sexes in total visits and licks. During place learning, male mice had a higher percent correct response than female mice, while female mice showed increases in licks and correct visits from day 1 to day 4. BAX KO mice made more visits overall but had a lower percent correct response than BAX WT mice on day 4. During reversal learning, male BAX KO mice showed a decrease in visits and had fewer visits with a lick than male BAX WT mice on day 4. In the A/B task, male BAX KO mice had higher discrimination scores than male BAX WT mice on day 5, while female BAX KO mice showed an initial advantage over female BAX WT mice. These results partially support our hypothesis that increasing neurogenesis would benefit male mice more. Overall, increasing the survival of newborn dentate granule cells does not improve learning in the same way across sexes and tasks.
articles.author: Tunc-Ozcan, E., Rodriguez, A. M.

articles.title: Sympathetic-to-microglia readouts in human brain single-nucleus data: sparse adrenergic receptor detection and age-associated homeostatic-to-inflammatory shifts in hippocampal microglia
articles.content: Stellate ganglion block (SGB) improves sleep in clinical populations, yet the mechanisms linking sympathetic activity to human microglial states remain untested. A prerequisite is to establish what sympathetic signaling readouts exist in human microglia and whether state composition changes in a disease-relevant physiological dimension. Using two public human single-nucleus datasets (the ROSMAP prefrontal cortex resource: 443 donors, 174,420 immune nuclei, 152,459 microglial nuclei, 12 published microglial states; and a hippocampal multiome cohort spanning adult lifespan: 40 donors, ages 20 - 100, 15,225 microglial nuclei), we quantified (i) adrenergic receptor and inflammatory/complement axis gene expression across microglial states, and (ii) donor-level trajectories of four microglial state signatures across age. Adrenergic receptors were barely detected: among nine receptor genes, only ADRB2 was detectable in 3.8 - 11.4% of nuclei, and no adrenergic receptor was state-specific. In contrast, inflammatory genes (nuclear factor-{kappa}B and interleukin modules) were strongly concentrated in one pro-inflammatory state (e.g., NFKB1 mean expression 1.47 vs 0.35 - 0.72 in other states; IL1B in 32.6% of nuclei vs 2 - 16% elsewhere), complement genes in a complement-enriched state, and lipid-metabolism/disease-associated genes in a distinct state. Across the adult lifespan, hippocampal microglia showed a donor-level decline of the homeostatic signature (mean score 0.70 to 0.38 across age quartiles; Spearman {rho} = -0.55, P = 2.6 * 10-4), with concordant rises of pro-inflammatory ({rho} = 0.37, P = 0.017) and disease-associated/lipid-metabolism ({rho} = 0.32, P = 0.045) signatures; an interferon signature showed no age trend. These results (a) indicate that human microglia lack a robust direct adrenergic receptor substrate at single-nucleus resolution, implying that sympathetic influence on microglia, if causal, is likely indirect or low-frequency, and (b) establish a donor-level, age-associated baseline shift toward inflammatory/trimming states in the human hippocampus. Together they define candidate readouts and the baseline against which chronic-sleep-disorder and neuromodulation-intervention studies (e.g., SGB) should be designed.
articles.author: Liang, M., Zeng, K.

articles.title: Target- and network-specific downstream effects of personalized precision transcranial magnetic stimulation: Evidence from concurrent functional neuroimaging
articles.content: Background: Personalized targeting of transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) based on functional connectivity (FC) to the subgenual anterior cingulate cortex (sgACC) is promising for depression treatment, but direct evidence that precisely engaging an individually defined FC target produces specific downstream modulation is lacking. Objective: To test whether stimulating individually defined cortical targets with strong negative or positive FC to sgACC/ventromedial prefrontal cortex (vmPFC) produces target- and network-specific downstream BOLD effects compared to nearby control targets. Methods: Twenty healthy participants underwent concurrent TMS-fMRI. For each participant, we identified a dorsolateral PFC target with strong negative FC and a dorsomedial PFC target with strong positive FC to sgACC/vmPFC as well as control targets with weaker sgACC/vmPFC-FC strength, but matched peripheral co-stimulation experience. Coil positions and orientations were optimized using electric field simulations. Single TMS pulses were applied during concurrent fMRI, and BOLD responses were compared between conditions. Results: Stimulation of negative FC targets produced significantly stronger negative BOLD modulation in sgACC/vmPFC and dorsomedial PFC compared to control targets. Positive FC targets showed no significant differences from controls. The spatial pattern of negative FC target-related BOLD effects significantly resembled a previously described convergent depression circuit, while positive FC targets produced an anticorrelated pattern. Conclusions: Personalized precision TMS targeting produces target- and network-specific downstream effects, supporting the mechanistic premise of FC-guided TMS.
articles.author: Lueckel, M., Radetz, A., Hassan, U., Yuen, K., Mueller-Dahlhaus, F., Kalisch, R., Bergmann, T. O.

articles.title: Hierarchical control of visual perceptual learning with model-synthesized stimuli
articles.content: Visual perceptual decisions depend on both how the visual system represents the stimuli and how those representations are read out to guide perception and behavior. Improved visual perception through training, a phenomenon known as Visual Perceptual Learning (VPL), has been partly attributed to adjustments of the readout weights across visual areas to reach better decisions. However, it has been difficult to test whether this reweighting remains at a late stage of the hierarchy or can amplify the readout of whichever hierarchical stage has the most informative representations for the training stimulus. Here, we leveraged DorsalNet, a hierarchical neural network model of the primate dorsal stream, to synthesize motion stimuli that selectively target early or late areas of the primate dorsal pathway. Human observers were trained to discriminate the synthesized stimuli over three days, and transfer was subsequently measured across retinal location and stimulus type. Training improved performance for both stimulus types (early- and late-stage targeting stimuli), but through different mechanisms. Training with late-stage stimuli significantly increased perceptual sensitivity, a gain that transferred across retinal locations. Training with early-stage stimuli produced only a weak, non-significant change in sensitivity; instead, it significantly reduced a conservative response bias, an effect that did not persist at the new retinal location. Specificity indices for stimulus location and type showed different patterns across stimulus categories. A DorsalNet-based model of VPL reproduced both the learning dynamics and these distinct specificity patterns most closely when the model readout was solely plastic for late, rather than early, model layers. Together, these results support a late-stage reweighting account of perceptual learning, in which readout from a preferred, late stage of the dorsal hierarchy is reweighted regardless of the trained stimulus. Under this account, stimuli well matched to the readout stage yield sensitivity gains, whereas poorly matched stimuli afford only weak sensory evidence, prompting observers to compensate by shifting their decision criteria.
articles.author: Valibeigi, Y., Pandey, A., Pack, C. C., Bakhtiari, S.

articles.title: The neural basis of unfamiliar face recognition in humans with fMRI frequency-tagging
articles.content: Faces provide the most diagnostic information for identifying individuals in humans. Understanding the neural mechanisms involved in face identity recognition (FIR) is particularly important for unfamiliar faces, for which identity cannot rely on encoded multimodal semantic associations. Here, we investigated the neural basis of FIR using an original frequency-tagging fMRI approach providing objective, sensitive, and reliable measures of face recognition. Ten human participants were presented within a rapid 6 Hz stream of natural images of a single unfamiliar identity in two conditions: (1) with the same face image across low-level changes (size, luminance, contrast) only, or (2) with images varying in background, size, head orientation, gaze direction, etc. Every 9 s during a 243 s run, seven images of different unfamiliar identities were introduced in bursts. For each participant and each condition, we recorded runs with upright and inverted faces. Analyses were performed within face-selective regions (defined from a frequency-tagging localizer) and in the Fourier domain, where individual face discrimination responses were objectively identified and quantified at the identity-change frequency (0.111 Hz). We observed robust image-based individual face discrimination responses across both conditions in core face-selective ventral regions (LatMidFG and IOG). In contrast, responses in early visual cortex and the pSTS were negligible in our second condition, which required generalization across viewpoint variations. In addition, the LatMidFG showed a reliable inversion effect, confirming that the observed responses cannot be attributed solely to low-level image differences. Overall, these findings highlight the value of fMRI frequency-tagging for objectively characterizing the cortical network underlying unfamiliar FIR, providing evidence for high-level discrimination and generalization of unfamiliar face identity in the human ventral occipito-temporal face-selective network.
articles.author: Laurent, M.-A., Durand, J.-B., Gao, X., Vayssiere, N., Berry, I., Rossion, B., Cottereau, B. R.

articles.title: The Dark Side of Light: Adolescent Light Exposure at Night Disrupts Hippocampal Clocks and Plasticity-Related Signaling in a Sex-Dependent Manner.
articles.content: In today's society, adolescents are being increasingly exposed to artificial blue light at night from electronic devices, raising concerns about its effects on brain development and mental health. The hippocampus, and specifically the dentate gyrus (DG) regulates memory formation and itself operates as a subordinate circadian oscillator detecting changes in the light environment. However, whether light at night during adolescence can impair hippocampal clock and function remains unknown. To begin exploring this, we exposed adolescent mice to a light cycle disruption (LCD) paradigm consisting of 12hrs of light followed by 5hrs of darkness and 7hrs of blue-enriched light for 5 consecutive days per week, followed by a standard 12 hours of light and 12 hours of darkness (12L:12D) for 2 days, over a 4-week period. Control animals were maintained under standard 12L:12D. Female and male mice were then tested for novel object recognition (NOR) and novel object location (NOL), and brain tissues were collected for clock gene expression, neuroplasticity markers, and dendritic spine analyses. We found that male mice exposed to LCD spent less time exploring novel objects and locations, and more time with familiar ones, a pattern consistent with impaired recognition and spatial memory, while female mice showed preserved memory performance despite LCD exposure. LCD-exposed male mice showed altered hippocampal daily expression rhythms of Clock and CRY2 levels compared to male control and LCD-exposed females. In addition, we found that LCD-exposed males exhibited reduced p-CREB expression along with reduced Bdnf and dendrite spines numbers in the DG. Interestingly, returning LCD-exposed males to standard 12L:12D conditions for 4 weeks were sufficient to reverse both the behavioral and molecular phenotypes. Together, these results suggest that chronic exposure to light at night during adolescence impairs memory in male mice, through alteration in hippocampal circadian clock regulation and plasticity-related mechanisms within the DG.
